presentingComplaint: Sudden collapse with massive haematemesis and dizziness
history: A 42-year-old man with known alcohol excess and chronic liver disease was brought to the emergency department after vomiting a large volume of fresh blood at home, followed by two further episodes en route. Witnesses report he became progressively pale, sweaty, and confused over 20 minutes prior to arrival. He denies chest pain or shortness of breath but is too drowsy to give a full history. Family report melena for the preceding two days and worsening fatigue. No known peptic ulcer disease; no NSAID or anticoagulant use reported. No fever or recent infection.
examination: Pale, diaphoretic, cool peripheries with delayed capillary refill (>4s). Drowsy but rousable, oriented to person only. Cool, clammy skin. Weak, thready radial pulse. No neck stiffness. Abdomen soft, mildly distended with shifting dullness consistent with ascites; no peritonism. Spider naevi and palmar erythema noted. Per-rectal exam confirms melena on glove.
imaging: Erect chest X-ray: no free air, no infiltrate
Bedside ultrasound: ascites present, no pericardial effusion, IVC collapsed with minimal respiratory variation consistent with hypovolaemia
differentialDiagnoses: Hypovolaemic (haemorrhagic) shock secondary to variceal bleed
Hypovolaemic shock secondary to bleeding peptic ulcer
Septic shock (SBP with GI bleed as red herring)
finalDiagnosis: Hypovolaemic shock due to acute upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage (suspected variceal bleed in cirrhosis)
citations: AASLD Practice Guidance — Portal Hypertensive Bleeding in Cirrhosis 2023
Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 (fluid resuscitation principles, applied by analogy for shock resuscitation)
contraindications: Avoid large-volume crystalloid over-resuscitation targeting supranormal BP in suspected variceal bleed — permissive/restrictive resuscitation strategy preferred until source control
Avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxic/antiplatelet agents
Avoid delaying blood product transfusion while awaiting crossmatch in exsanguinating haemorrhage — use emergency-release O-negative blood
edgeCases: Cirrhotic patients may have blunted tachycardic response due to non-selective beta-blocker use, masking severity of shock
Coagulopathy and thrombocytopenia from liver disease compound haemorrhagic shock and complicate resuscitation
Encephalopathy from hepatic dysfunction and/or hypoperfusion may mimic or mask hypovolaemic shock's altered sensorium

'hypovolemic_shock' is the closest engine id for this presentation, but the underlying trigger (variceal bleed in cirrhosis) also maps to 'variceal_bleed' and 'decomp_cirrhosis' as clinically relevant differentials/co-diagnoses
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag haemorrhagic hypovolaemic shock from a likely variceal source in a cirrhotic patient, prioritizing airway protection, massive transfusion protocol activation, restrictive fluid/blood resuscitation, and urgent endoscopy over vasopressor escalation.
expectedNextQuestions: Is there a history of known oesophageal varices or prior variceal bleeding?
What is the estimated total blood loss and time course?
Has massive transfusion protocol been activated and is crossmatched blood available?
Is urgent upper GI endoscopy available within the recommended window?
Is terlipressin/octreotide and prophylactic antibiotic (per cirrhosis GI bleed protocol) indicated?
expectedInvestigations: Full blood count, coagulation profile, liver function tests
Group and crossmatch / massive transfusion panel
Serum lactate and venous/arterial blood gas
Bedside ultrasound (IVC assessment, FAST if trauma suspected)
